title: Molecular Hydrogen: an Emerging Therapeutic Medical Gas for Brain Disorders.
abstract: Oxidative stress and neuroinflammation are the main physiopathological changes involved in the initiation and progression of various neurodegenerative disorders or brain injuries. Since the landmark finding reported in 2007 found that hydrogen reduced the levels of peroxynitrite anions and hydroxyl free radicals in ischemic stroke, molecular hydrogen's antioxidative and anti-inflammatory effects have aroused widespread interest. Due to its excellent antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, hydrogen therapy via different routes of administration exhibits great therapeutic potential for a wide range of brain disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, depression, anxiety, traumatic brain injury, ischemic stroke, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis. This paper reviews the routes for hydrogen administration, the effects of hydrogen on the previously mentioned brain disorders, and the primary mechanism underlying hydrogen's neuroprotection. Finally, we discuss hydrogen therapy's remaining issues and challenges in brain disorders. We conclude that understanding the exact molecular target, finding novel routes, and determining the optimal dosage for hydrogen administration is critical for future studies and applications.

title: Post-ischemic inhibition of the mitochondrial Ca2+ uniporter with Ru265 protects in ex vivo and in vivo models of cerebral ischemia.
abstract: Brain ischemia is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in the aging population, yet no effective neuroprotective interventions currently exist. This therapeutic gap stems from two key challenges: the inability to deliver neuroprotective drugs before reperfusion and limited understanding of post-reperfusion events leading to delayed neurodegeneration. Zn2+ is an important contributor to ischemic brain injury, with mitochondrial Zn2+ uptake playing a central role in its neurotoxic effects. Ongoing Zn2+ accumulation occurs through the mitochondrial Ca2+ uniporter (MCU) in selectively vulnerable CA1 neurons after transient ischemia, contributing to delayed mitochondrial dysfunction. We previously demonstrated that post-ischemic administration of the non-selective MCU antagonist, ruthenium red attenuated neuronal damage in both an ex vivo oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD) mouse brain slice model and in an in vivo rat cardiac arrest (CA) model. In the present study, we test post-ischemic treatment with Ru265, a novel selective MCU blocker, in both ischemic models. In the slice model, OGD induced delayed Zn2+ accumulation in CA1 neuronal mitochondria (as previously reported), followed by late-onset persistent mitochondrial depolarization and sustained elevation of cytoplasmic Ca2+ levels, indicating loss of Ca2+ homeostasis. Application of Ru265 after OGD termination inhibited the mitochondrial Zn2+ accumulation and largely prevented subsequent mitochondrial depolarization and loss of cytosolic Ca2+ homeostasis. In the CA model, intravenous Ru265 administration during cardiopulmonary resuscitation largely mitigated mitochondrial damage, markedly reduced neuronal injury and improved behavioral outcomes 20-24 h after ischemia. These findings suggest that post-ischemic MCU blockade may constitute a promising neuroprotective therapeutic strategy.
englishSummary: Brain ischemia is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in the aging population, yet no effective neuroprotective interventions currently exist. This therapeutic gap stems from two key challenges: the inability to deliver neuroprotective drugs before reperfusion and limited understanding of post-reperfusion events leading to delayed neurodegeneration. Zn2+ is an important contributor to ischemic brain injury, with mitochondrial Zn2+ uptake playing a central role in its neurotoxic effects.

title: PVT1 inhibition alleviates cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury and is associated with stroke diagnosis and severity via MyD88-mediated inflammatory signaling.
abstract: Cerebral ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury is a major cause of neurological disability. This study investigated the role of lncRNA PVT1 in I/R-induced cerebral injury and its clinical relevance. MCAO/reperfusion mouse and OGD/R neuronal cell models were established. Neurological function, infarct volume, brain edema, and neuronal apoptosis were assessed. For clinical validation, 50 acute ischemic stroke patients and 50 healthy controls were enrolled. Serum PVT1/miR-187-3p were measured by qRT-PCR; plasma MyD88 and inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-18) by ELISA. Machine learning (Random Forest) and correlation analyses were performed to evaluate diagnostic utility and relationships with clinical severity (NIHSS score, infarct volume). PVT1 was significantly upregulated under I/R both in vivo and in vitro. Clinically, AIS patients showed markedly elevated PVT1 (3.92 vs. 1.02, p < 0.0001) and reduced miR-187-3p (0.42 vs. 1.01, p < 0.0001), with increased MyD88 and inflammatory cytokines (all p < 0.001). The Random Forest model achieved AUC = 0.92, with PVT1 as the top predictor. PVT1 correlated positively with MyD88 (r = 0.68, p < 0.001) and NIHSS score (r = 0.61, p < 0.001). PVT1 silencing in MCAO mice significantly improved neurological function, reduced infarct volume and brain edema, and attenuated neuronal apoptosis (all p < 0.01). Mechanistically, PVT1 sponged miR-187-3p to derepress MyD88/TLR4 signaling, which was reversed by miR-187-3p restoration. In vivo rescue experiments confirmed that miR-187-3p antagomir reversed the protective effects of PVT1 silencing across multiple endpoints. PVT1 inhibition protects against cerebral I/R injury by restoring miR-187-3p and blocking the MyD88/TLR4 pathway. PVT1 and its downstream axis are associated with stroke diagnosis and severity, and represent promising therapeutic targets and diagnostic biomarkers for ischemic stroke.
englishSummary: Cerebral ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury is a major cause of neurological disability. This study investigated the role of lncRNA PVT1 in I/R-induced cerebral injury and its clinical relevance. MCAO/reperfusion mouse and OGD/R neuronal cell models were established.

title: Association of Advanced Age With Functional Recovery After Endovascular Thrombectomy in Patients With Large-core Ischemic Stroke.
abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Evidence supporting endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) for large-core ischemic stroke has expanded, but outcomes in patients aged ≥80 years remain insufficiently characterized. We evaluated outcomes after EVT in this population, with particular attention to prestroke disability-adjusted functional recovery. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective study included patients with anterior-circulation large vessel occlusion and large-core stroke (Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score 0 to 5 or CT perfusion core volume ≥50 mL) treated with EVT between October 2019 and September 2025. The primary outcome was prestroke disability-adjusted functional recovery, defined as 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) ≤ prestroke mRS + 1. RESULTS: Among 377 patients, 75 were aged ≥80 years, and 302 were <80 years. Functional recovery occurred in 14.7% and 18.9%, respectively. Age ≥80 years was not significantly associated with functional recovery (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.00; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.45-2.22; p = 0.992). Patients aged ≥80 years had lower odds of mRS 0 to 3 (aOR, 0.41; 95% CI, 0.21-0.79) and higher odds of mortality (aOR, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.01-3.16). Successful reperfusion and hemorrhagic outcomes did not differ significantly between groups. Each 10-year increase in age was associated with lower odds of functional recovery (aOR, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.46-0.77). CONCLUSION: Among selected patients aged ≥80 years with large-core ischemic stroke, successful reperfusion and functional recovery remained achievable after EVT, despite poorer conventional functional outcomes and higher mortality. Advancing age was associated with progressively worse outcomes when modeled continuously. These findings support individualized prognostic assessment after EVT rather than reliance on chronological age alone.

title: Microglia promote infiltration and polarization of macrophages in cerebral ischemia‑reperfusion via the reactive oxygen species‑SPI1‑CCL9 axis.
abstract: in vitro in vivo in vitro The aim of the present study was to investigate the role of microglia in promoting macrophage infiltration and polarization during cerebral ischemia‑reperfusion (I/R) injury through the reactive oxygen species (ROS)‑Spi‑1 proto‑oncogene (SPI1)‑chemokine (C‑C motif) ligand 9 (CCL9) signalling axis. Using a cerebral I/Randmodel, microglial activation and macrophage dynamics were assessed. ROS levels were quantified, and SPI1 expression in microglia was analysed. CCL9 secretion was measured, and its impact on macrophage migration and polarization was evaluated. CCL9 antibody and RNA interference approaches were used to interrogate the signalling pathway. Following cerebral I/R, microglial activation led to increased ROS production, and increased SPI1 and CCL9 expression. This, in turn, increased CCL9 secretion, which attracted macrophages to the site of ischemia and promoted their polarization towards a pro‑inflammatory phenotype. Inhibition of the ROS‑SPI1‑CCL9 axis significantly reduced macrophage infiltration and altered their polarization state. The results of the present study demonstrated that microglia facilitated macrophage infiltration and polarization in cerebral I/R via the ROS‑SPI1‑CCL9 axis, highlighting a potential therapeutic target for mitigating neuroinflammatory damage after a cerebral ischemic stroke.

Using a cerebral I/Randmodel, microglial activation and macrophage dynamics were assessed. ROS levels were quantified, and SPI1 expression in microglia was analysed.

title: Ghrelin treatment is associated with attenuated microglial inflammation and preserved mitochondrial integrity after cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury (CI/RI) causes neurological disability. Microglial inflammation and mitochondrial apoptosis are key pathological events. Ghrelin's role in these processes following CI/RI remains unclear. OBJECTIVES: To examine whether ghrelin treatment is associated with reduced microglial inflammation and preserved mitochondrial integrity in CI/RI models, using in vitro OGD/R primary microglia and in vivo MCAO rat models. METHODS: Primary microglia underwent OGD/R (8 h/24 h) with ghrelin (0.1-1 mM). Cell viability, apoptosis, GHSR, inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8), ROS, ATP, mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), and ultrastructure were measured. Rats underwent MCAO (2 h/24 h) and received ghrelin (50 μg/kg/d, i.p.) or saline for 7 days. Infarct volume, histology, IBA-1, mitochondrial complexes I/IV, cytochrome c distribution, NF-κB p65 translocation, TNF-α/IL-1β/IL-6, and Bcl-2/Bax/Caspase-9 were assessed. RESULTS: In OGD/R-exposed microglia, ghrelin dose-dependently attenuated viability loss and apoptosis, restored GHSR, reduced TNF-α/IL-6/IL-8, lowered ROS, increased ATP, and preserved ΔΨm and ultrastructure. In MCAO rats, ghrelin treatment was associated with smaller infarct volume, less neuronal damage, lower IBA-1, restored ATP and complexes I/IV, increased mitochondrial cytochrome c retention, reduced NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation, decreased TNF-α/IL-1β/IL-6, and altered Bcl-2/Bax/Caspase-9 (higher Bcl-2 and full-length Caspase-9, lower Bax). CONCLUSION: In both models, ghrelin treatment correlates with attenuated microglial inflammation and preserved mitochondrial integrity. These findings indicate a potential protective association of ghrelin against CI/RI.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury (CI/RI) causes neurological disability. Microglial inflammation and mitochondrial apoptosis are key pathological events. Ghrelin's role in these processes following CI/RI remains unclear.

title: Proanthocyanidin ameliorates BCCAO-induced neuroinflammation in cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) in rats by targeting NF-κB/NLRP3 inflammasome pathway.
abstract: Cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) is a major cause of mortality and long-term neurological disability, characterized by excessive oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and neuronal degeneration following the restoration of cerebral blood flow. The present study investigated the neuroprotective effects of proanthocyanidin (PAC) against bilateral common carotid artery occlusion (BCCAO)-induced cerebral ischemia in Wistar albino rats, with particular emphasis on the NF-κB/NLRP3 inflammasome signaling pathway. Rats subjected to BCCAO received PAC at two dose levels or standard therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel). Neurological and cognitive functions were evaluated using the rotarod, actophotometer, and elevated plus maze tests. Biochemical assays were performed to determine oxidative stress markers and antioxidant enzyme activities, while histopathological examination assessed neuronal integrity. The molecular mechanism was further investigated by Western blot analysis and densitometric quantification of NF-κB (p65), NLRP3, and caspase-1 protein expression. BCCAO significantly impaired motor coordination, locomotor activity, and memory retention, accompanied by increased lipid peroxidation, myeloperoxidase, and acetylcholinesterase activities, depletion of endogenous antioxidants (glutathione, superoxide dismutase, and catalase), and marked neuronal degeneration in the hippocampal and cortical regions. PAC treatment significantly improved behavioral performance, restored antioxidant defense, reduced oxidative stress and biochemical alterations, and preserved neuronal architecture in a dose-dependent manner. Western blot analysis demonstrated that PAC markedly downregulated the overexpression of NF-κB (p65), NLRP3, and caspase-1 proteins, indicating suppression of NF-κB/NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated neuroinflammation. Overall, PAC exhibited significant neuroprotective efficacy comparable to aspirin plus clopidogrel, suggesting that its beneficial effects are mediated through the attenuation of oxidative stress and the inhibition of NF-κB/NLRP3 inflammasome signaling. These findings support PAC as a promising phytotherapeutic candidate for the management of cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury.

The present study investigated the neuroprotective effects of proanthocyanidin (PAC) against bilateral common carotid artery occlusion (BCCAO)-induced cerebral ischemia in Wistar albino rats, with particular emphasis on the NF-κB/NLRP3 inflammasome signaling pathway. Rats subjected to BCCAO received PAC at two dose levels or standard therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel).

title: ATP-sensitive potassium channel openers inhibit the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps to protect against neuroinflammation in ischemic stroke.
abstract: Neuroinflammation is a key contributor to brain injury and poor functional recovery after ischemic stroke, yet no clinically approved therapy targets the neutrophil extracellular trap (NET)-cGAS-STING axis that drives it. This study investigates the effects of the clinically used K-ATP channel opener nicorandil on neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation and evaluates its potential to attenuate NET-cGAS-STING-associated neuroinflammation. A mouse model of middle cerebral artery occlusion and reperfusion (MCAO/R) and BV-2 microglial cell oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R) were used to assess NET formation, cGAS-STING pathway activation, inflammatory responses, and neurological injury. Significant increases in NET markers, such as MPO-DNA and CitH3, were found in plasma and brain tissue after MCAO/R. This was accompanied by elevated TNF-α, IL-6、IL-1β, brain edema, neuronal apoptosis, and neurological deficits. Both DNase I-mediated NET degradation and Nicorandil treatment reduced NET formation, suppressed microglial activation, lowered phosphorylation of STING and TBK1, and alleviated brain infarction, neuronal death, and impairment. In vitro, exogenous NETs enhanced OGD/R-induced cGAS-STING activation and IL-1β release, effects reversed by DNase I and Nicorandil. In summary, extracellular DNA associated with NETs promotes microglial cGAS-STING activation and contributes to neuroinflammatory injury after stroke. Nicorandil exerts neuroprotective effects by inhibiting the upstream formation of NETs and attenuating this signaling axis, suggesting a promising and readily translatable therapeutic strategy for ischemic stroke.

title: Niwan Bazhen acupuncture activates CLEC3B-Mediated PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway to suppress autophagy and exerts neuroprotection against ischemic stroke.
abstract: Ischemic stroke (IS) is one of the leading causes of disability and mortality worldwide. Excessive autophagy triggered by cerebral ischemia exacerbates neuronal apoptosis and necrosis. Acupuncture at Niwan Bazhen (Acu) has unique advantages in stroke rehabilitation, and our previous studies have demonstrated its ability to alleviate neuronal apoptosis after IS. However, the mechanisms underlying its therapeutic effects remain elusive. Transcriptomic microarray expression profiling revealed that C-type lectin domain family 3 member B (CLEC3B) was significantly downregulated in the brain of middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO/R) rats, and this downregulation was reversed by Acu. Lentivirus-mediated overexpression of CLEC3B improved neurological function, reduced cerebral infarction, and alleviated cerebral edema in MCAO/R rats, and decreased neuronal apoptosis in the peri-infarct cortex. Western blot analysis demonstrated that CLEC3B overexpression activated the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway, reduced the LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, and decreased autophagosome numbers. Conversely, knockdown of CLEC3B nearly abolished the neuroprotective effects of Acu in MCAO/R rats. In vitro, CLEC3B dificiency inhibited the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway and impaired autophagic flux in rat cortical neurons under oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R) conditions. Treatment of OGD/R-exposed rat cortical neurons with recombinant CLEC3B protein or CLEC3B-overexresing lentivirus activated the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway and inhibited autophagy, an effect that was abrogated by the PI3K inhibitor LY294002. Collectively, these findings indicate that CLEC3B, as a core target of Acu regulation, exerts neuroprotection against IS by inhibiting excessive neuronal autophagy via activating the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway.
englishSummary: Ischemic stroke (IS) is one of the leading causes of disability and mortality worldwide. Excessive autophagy triggered by cerebral ischemia exacerbates neuronal apoptosis and necrosis. Acupuncture at Niwan Bazhen (Acu) has unique advantages in stroke rehabilitation, and our previous studies have demonstrated its ability to alleviate neuronal apoptosis after IS.

title: Characteristic Dihydrophenanthrenes from Spiranthes sinensis with Therapeutic Potential for Ischemic Stroke.
abstract: Spiranthes sinensis, known as "Panlongshen", is an edible traditional Chinese medicine, widely used in herbal teas and health-promoting foods. In this study, we investigated the neuroprotective properties of S. sinensis against ischemic stroke for the first time. Bioactivity-guided isolation yielded 19 dihydrophenanthrenes, including 9 undescribed compounds (7a/7b, 9-11, 12a/12b-13a/13b). These dihydrophenanthrenes demonstrated significant antineuroinflammatory activity against NO production in LPS-induced BV-2 microglia cells, with IC50 values ranging from 1.5 to 34.8 μM, which were greater than that of the positive drug (minocycline, IC50: 34.9 μM). Furthermore, coelonin (2) reduced inflammatory cytokines in BV-2 microglia and preserved PC12 cells' viability under oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation. Mechanistic investigations revealed that coelonin (2) exerts its antineuroinflammatory effects by targeting MAP3K7 and suppressing the NF-κB signaling cascade. In vivo, coelonin alleviated ischemic-reperfusion injury after MCAO. These findings revealed the neuroprotective and anti-ischemic stroke effects of S. sinensis and identified dihydrophenanthrenes as its key active constituents.
englishSummary: Spiranthes sinensis, known as "Panlongshen", is an edible traditional Chinese medicine, widely used in herbal teas and health-promoting foods. In this study, we investigated the neuroprotective properties of S. sinensis against ischemic stroke for the first time.

title: Stage-Associated Efficacy of Systemically Administered Neural Stem Cell-Derived Exosomes in Ischemic Stroke through the Prevention of Cx43 Degradation.
abstract: Ischemic stroke pathology is highly dynamic, making the optimal timing for biological interventions highly elusive. This study investigated the stage-associated therapeutic efficacy of neural stem cell-derived exosomes (NSC-Exos) for cerebral ischemia-reperfusion. The in vivo evaluations identified a restricted therapeutic window closely associated with the temporal evolution of the ischemic microenvironment. Early exosome intervention (4 or 24 h post-ischemia) significantly reduced infarct volume, restored blood-brain barrier integrity, and improved neurological functional recovery. In contrast, delayed administration (48 h) failed to reduce the mortality rate and provide meaningful neuroprotection. To examine the molecular basis of this time dependence, we integrated temporal proteomic profiling of the ischemic penumbra with small RNA sequencing of NSC-Exos. The analytical and functional data suggest that early NSC-Exo delivery transfers miR-9-5p to suppress Nedd4 expression, thereby restoring the Connexin 43 protein pool and stabilizing the astrocytic network to halt initial microenvironmental collapse. Collectively, this study underscores the critical importance of intervention timing and provides a potential translational strategy for utilizing NSC-Exos as a targeted, stage-specific therapy in acute ischemic stroke.

This study investigated the stage-associated therapeutic efficacy of neural stem cell-derived exosomes (NSC-Exos) for cerebral ischemia-reperfusion. The in vivo evaluations identified a restricted therapeutic window closely associated with the temporal evolution of the ischemic microenvironment.

title: Thrombus stiffness depends on occlusion site and influences thrombectomy outcomes in acute ischemic stroke.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Only 60% of patients with acute ischemic stroke (AIS) achieve successful reperfusion after the first endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) attempt. In vitro studies have shown that thrombus stiffness influences thrombus-device interaction and retrieval efficacy. This prospective observational study investigates how thrombus stiffness relates to clinical factors, thrombus imaging characteristics and histological composition. It further explores the association between thrombus stiffness and EVT success, as measured by the modified first-pass reperfusion (mFPR). PATIENTS AND METHODS: A total of 281 thrombus samples were collected from 51 AIS patients undergoing EVT. Thrombus stiffness was quantified using compressive mechanical testing, composition from histological staining and radiological characteristics from pre-interventional non-contrast computed tomography (CT) and CT angiography. Statistical analysis was performed using linear and logistic mixed-effects regression models. RESULTS: Thrombi retrieved from the proximal M2 segment of the middle cerebral artery showed significant lower stiffness (0.236 kPa, 95% CI, 0.136-0.409) compared to those from the M1 segment (0.760 kPa, 95% CI, 0.492-1.174) and from the ICA (1.106 kPa, 95% CI, 0.558-2.192). Occlusion location was the strongest clinical marker of thrombus stiffness. Adjusted mFPR probability was 40.4% (95% CI, 24.5-67.0) for thrombi retrieved from the ICA, 89.7% (95% CI, 79.5-97.0) for M1 occlusions, and 53.0% (95% CI, 30.8-84.7) for M2 occlusions. CONCLUSION: Thrombi in distal vessels of the anterior cerebral circulation are significantly softer than those in proximal intracranial arteries. First-pass EVT success is lower for the stiffest thrombi from the ICA and for the softest thrombi from M2, providing a foundation for future biomechanically informed thrombus removal strategies to optimise AIS treatment.
englishSummary: INTRODUCTION: Only 60% of patients with acute ischemic stroke (AIS) achieve successful reperfusion after the first endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) attempt. In vitro studies have shown that thrombus stiffness influences thrombus-device interaction and retrieval efficacy. This prospective observational study investigates how thrombus stiffness relates to clinical factors, thrombus imaging characteristics and histological composition.

title: Early Acupuncture Following Thrombolysis in Acute Ischemic Stroke: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials on Efficacy and Safety.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Intravenous thrombolysis is standard for acute ischemic stroke (AIS), but many patients still have poor outcomes. Acupuncture may confer additional neuroprotection, yet its safety and efficacy when initiated early post-thrombolysis remain unclear. METHODS: 2 A systematic search of databases and registries was conducted from inception to March 31, 2026, for randomized controlled trials comparing thrombolysis plus acupuncture with thrombolysis plus conventional post-thrombolytic care in AIS patients within 14 days of onset. Meta-analyses were performed using mean differences (MD) or risk ratios (RR) with 95% CIs. Heterogeneity was assessed with the Istatistic; publication bias was evaluated via Egger's test. Pre-specified subgroup analyses were conducted. RESULTS: Ten trials (1116 patients) were included. Adjunctive acupuncture reduced neurological deficit (NIHSS MD -2.90, 95% CI -3.62 to -2.17), improved activities of daily living (Barthel Index MD 12.07, 95% CI 8.10-16.03), and increased clinical response (RR 1.16, 95% CI 1.11-1.21; all p < 0.001). Adverse events did not differ significantly (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.25-1.08). Only one study reported symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (zero acupuncture vs. six control). Benefits were consistent across subgroups. CONCLUSION: In AIS patients receiving thrombolysis, acupuncture initiated early following thrombolysis improves neurological and functional outcomes. In available safety data, adverse events did not differ significantly between groups; however, systematic surveillance for symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was lacking in most trials. These findings support further rigorous evaluation of early post-thrombolysis acupuncture in adequately monitored randomized trials. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: PROSPERO CRD420261358943.

title: Intranuclear localisation of KLF3-AS1 under the balance of histone acetylation and methylation in BMSCs ameliorates cerebral ischaemia‒reperfusion injury by preserving microglial mitochondrial function and inhibiting inflammatory polarisation.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Ischaemic stroke occurs when blood flow to the brain is obstructed. Rapid restoration of blood supply frequently induces cerebral ischaemia‒reperfusion injury (CIRI). Bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC)-derived exosomes exhibit promising therapeutic potential for CIRI. In-depth exploration of their therapeutic mechanisms holds crucial significance for CIRI management. METHODS: 2+ The middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO) model was established in mice. An in vitro ischaemic stroke model was established by treating BV-2 cells with oxygen‒glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R). Exosomes were isolated from BMSCs and intranasally administrated into mice or added into BV-2 cells. Neurological deficits, grasping and coordination function were evaluated. Cell viability, apoptosis, proliferation and migration were examined. The localisation of KLF3-AS1 was examined by combined staining of immunofluorescence and fluorescence in situ hybridisation. Intracellular Caand adenosine triphosphate levels, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species and membrane potential were assessed. RESULTS: KLF3-AS1 enhanced BMSC viability, proliferation and migration, accompanied by epigenetic reprogramming at its promoter characterised by increased H3K27 acetylation (H3K27Ac) and decreased H3K27 trimethylation (H3K27Me3). BMSC-derived KLF3-AS1-enriched exosomes indicated therapeutic efficacy in both in vivo and in vitro models of cerebral ischaemia. In MCAO-induced mice, these exosomes alleviated neurological deficits and shifted microglial polarisation from pro-inflammatory M1-like to anti-inflammatory M2-like phenotypes. Similar effects were observed in OGD/R-treated BV-2 microglia, where KLF3-AS1-enriched exosomes attenuated oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction while upregulating Silent Information Regulator 3 (SIRT3) expression. Mechanistically, KLF3-AS1 facilitated ETS Variant Transcription Factor 4 (ETV4) nuclear translocation to activate SIRT3 transcription in microglia, and inhibition of SIRT3 abolished the neuroprotective effects of exosomal KLF3-AS1. CONCLUSION: BMSC-derived exosomes delivering KLF3-AS1 ameliorates CIRI by preserving microglial mitochondrial function and inhibiting inflammatory polarisation, highlighting KLF3-AS1 as a critical epigenetic regulator and exosome-mediated therapeutic agent for CIRI through the ETV4/SIRT3 axis. KEY POINTS/HIGHLIGHTS: KLF3-AS1 enhances bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC) function via promoter H3K27Ac/H3K27Me3 reprogramming. KLF3‑AS1 directly binds ETS Variant Transcription Factor 4 (ETV4) to activate Silent Information Regulator 3 (SIRT3), preserving mitochondrial integrity. BMSC‑derived exosomal KLF3‑AS1 promotes M2 microglial polarisation and ameliorates cerebral ischaemia-reperfusion injury.

Bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC)-derived exosomes exhibit promising therapeutic potential for CIRI.

title: Lipid Droplet-Associated Hsp70 Palmitoylation Drives Lysosomal Dysfunction in Ischemic Stroke.
abstract: Lipid droplet (LDs) accumulate in glial cells across neurodegenerative and ischemic brain pathologies. LDs modulate cellular stress via organelle crosstalk, particularly with lysosomes, whose dysfunction and cathepsin leakage drive glial activation after cerebral ischemia. However, the molecular link between accumulated LDs and lysosomes in pathological glial activation remains incompletely understood. Using a mouse middle cerebral artery occlusion ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) model and oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/Re) cell models, we found that both LD signal intensity and lysosomal cathepsin B leakage progressively increased from day 1 to day 14 after I/R. Etomoxir, an inhibitor of carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 A (CPT1A), the rate-limiting enzyme for fatty acid β-oxidation, aggravated I/R-induced LD accumulation and lysosomal damage in glial cells. Exogenous LDs derived from OGD/Re-treated glial cells aggravated lysosomal damage and promoted the proliferation of astrocytes and microglia. LD accumulation was associated with Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution of Hsp70 from lysosomes to the extracellular space, leading to lysosomal damage and reactive glial activation. Mechanistically, using multiple genetic and pharmacological approaches, including Plin3 knockdown, an Hsp70 palmitoylation‑site mutant, recombinant human Hsp70 (rhHsp70), as well as a pan-palmitoylation inhibitor and TLR2/4 antagonist, we consistently validated that Plin3, an LD surface protein, interacts with lysosomal Hsp70, causing Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution, and lysosomal damage. Extracellular Hsp70 activates TLR2/4 on glial cells, promoting cell proliferation and pro-inflammatory cytokine release. Collectively, these findings indicate that pathological LDs interacting with lysosomes drive Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution, causing lysosomal impairment and astrogliosis in ischemic stroke. We uncover Hsp70 palmitoylation as a potential drug target for ischemic stroke therapy.

title: Atractylenolide I ameliorates microglia-mediated cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury by suppressing the TLR4/NF-κB/NLRP3 inflammasome axis.
abstract: UNLABELLED: Atractylodes macrocephala Inflammatory responses play a pivotal role in cerebral ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury, with microglia‑driven neuroinflammation further exacerbating neuronal damage. Atractylenolide I (ATR-I), a natural bioactive compound derived from, exhibits anti-inflammatory properties by modulating signaling cascades. Nevertheless, its potential neuroprotective effects against cerebral I/R injury require further investigation.This study examined ATR-I's impact on microglial involvement in I/R-induced injury using two models: (i) BV2 microglial cells subjected to OGD/R in vitro, and (ii) a murine model of MCAO/R in vivo. Assessments included cellular viability, apoptosis, and inflammatory mediator secretion in vitro, while infarct volume, neurological function, neuronal apoptosis, and microglial activation were evaluated in vivo. Molecular mechanisms were explored via western blot and immunofluorescence. ATR-I substantially enhanced cellular survival while reducing apoptotic cell death and suppressing inflammatory cytokines secretion in OGD/R-treated BV2 cells. On the mechanistic front, ATR-I blocked two key inflammatory pathways: NLRP3 inflammasome activation and the TLR4/NF-κB signaling cascade. In experiments using the MCAO/R model, ATR-I treatment reduced infarct extent, improved neurological recovery, decreased neuronal apoptosis, and suppressed microglial activation-effects mediated by suppressing the TLR4/NF-κB/NLRP3 pathway. The ability of ATR-I to counteract cerebral I/R injury arises from its suppressive effect on the TLR4/NF‑κB/NLRP3 cascade. On account of this effect, ATR-I is considered a promising therapeutic agent for acute cerebral ischemia therapy, given its capacity to modulate microglia‑mediated neuroinflammatory reactions. title: Molecular Networks of Cell Death in Ischemic Stroke: From Mechanisms to Interventions.
abstract: Ischemic stroke involves a complex network of interconnected processes, including bioenergetic failure, excitotoxicity, ionic dyshomeostasis involving Na+, K+, Ca2+, and Cl-, oxidative stress, DNA damage, and neurovascular dysfunction. Apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis, and parthanatos contribute to experimental ischemic injury with different levels of mechanistic support. Autophagy primarily maintains cellular homeostasis and modulates these pathways. Autophagy-dependent cell death requires separate evidence that the autophagic machinery causes death. These processes operate across the ischemic core and penumbra and evolve during ischemia, reperfusion, and recovery. Their effects extend beyond neurons to microglia, astrocytes, brain microvascular endothelial cells, pericytes, and other neurovascular components. This narrative review evaluates pathway execution, shared molecular nodes, and the spatial and temporal limits of the available evidence. It emphasizes receptor-complex regulation, mitochondrial and lysosomal function, phospholipid peroxidation, DNA damage, and inflammatory signaling as points of convergence. Preclinical interventions are assessed according to their models, molecular endpoints, and functional outcomes. A cell- and stage-specific network perspective supports the development of targeted therapies, while the efficacy and safety of coordinated pathway intervention in patients remain to be established.

title: Remote ischemic preconditioning protects against cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury through lactate-dependent AMPK/ULK1 signaling and autophagy.
abstract: Cerebral ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury is a major contributor to ischemic cerebral damage and poor functional outcomes following ischemic stroke, and effective neuroprotective strategies remain limited. Remote ischemic preconditioning (RIPC) has emerged as a promising, noninvasive approach; however, its underlying mechanisms are incompletely understood. Here, we investigated whether lactate serves as a key metabolic mediator linking RIPC to neuroprotection through regulation of autophagy. Using an oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R) model in PC12 cells and a middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) model in rats, we demonstrate that I/R impairs autophagic flux, as evidenced by p62 accumulation and reduced LC3-II and Beclin-1 expression, leading to increased cellular apoptosis and injury. Lactate supplementation restored autophagic flux, enhanced cell viability, and suppressed apoptosis under OGD/R conditions. Mechanistically, lactate activated the AMPK/ULK1 signaling pathway, whereas pharmacological inhibition of AMPK or ULK1 attenuated lactate-induced autophagy and cytoprotection. In vivo, RIPC elevated plasma and cerebral lactate levels, activated AMPK/ULK1 signaling, promoted autophagy, reduced infarct volume, and improved acute neurological outcomes. Notably, blockade of lactate transport or inhibition of AMPK/ULK1 signaling attenuated these protective effects. Collectively, our findings suggest that lactate serves as an important mediator of RIPC-induced neuroprotection and reveal a novel lactate-AMPK/ULK1-autophagy axis that mitigates cerebral I/R injury. These results provide mechanistic insight into RIPC and suggest potential therapeutic targets for ischemic stroke.

Remote ischemic preconditioning (RIPC) has emerged as a promising, noninvasive approach; however, its underlying mechanisms are incompletely understood. Here, we investigated whether lactate serves as a key metabolic mediator linking RIPC to neuroprotection through regulation of autophagy.

title: Performance of the Lausanne Ischemic Stroke Pathway prehospital triage system in identifying acute reperfusion candidates: a quality-control study.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Accurate identification is one of the cornerstones of prehospital care for patients with suspected acute ischaemic stroke (AIS). In the Lausanne Ischemic Stroke Pathway triage system, emergency medical service (EMS) providers use dedicated criteria to identify acute reperfusion candidates and call a coordinated medical team (CMT, including a neurologist and an emergency physician), which can activate the stroke code pathway. The objective of this study was to evaluate the performance of the system in identifying acute reperfusion candidates. METHODS: This was a retrospective single-centre quality-control study conducted in a Swiss university-based stroke centre, from 1 January 2019 to 31 May 2022. Inclusion criteria were patients aged ≥18 years, for whom the EMS called the CMT or patients with AIS eligible for acute reperfusion managed by the EMS. The main outcomes were the performance of both the EMS and the CMT in detecting AIS patients eligible for acute reperfusion, as assessed through their respective under- and overtriage rates. A secondary outcome was the identification of alternative diagnoses in overtriaged patients. RESULTS: Of 1071 patients included, the EMS phone-contacted the CMT for 937 (87.5%) of them. Among the 1071 patients, 440 (41%) had an AIS eligible for reperfusion. The system's undertriage rate was 30% (133 patients without stroke pathway activation among the 440 patients with an AIS eligible for acute reperfusion). The undertriage rates were 21% for the EMS and 11% for the CMT. The overtriage rates were 63% for the EMS and 57% for the CMT. The main alternative diagnoses in overtriaged patients were seizures (14%), intracranial haemorrhages (9.9%) and functional disorders (6.5%). CONCLUSION: Undertriage and overtriage rates were relatively high, but both were reduced by the CMT call, highlighting the added value of a second expert assessment step, with a higher level of expertise. Concerning overtriage, a better prehospital identification of alternative diagnoses, such as seizures or functional disorders, could help to better classify our patients.

title: Diffusion-weighted imaging reversal after reperfusion therapy in acute ischemic stroke: associations with white matter hyperintensities and cerebral microbleeds.
abstract: BACKGROUND: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) and cerebral microbleeds (CMBs) are common MRI markers of chronic small-vessel brain injury and have been associated with adverse outcomes after ischemic stroke. However, whether these markers influence early ischemic tissue reversibility following reperfusion therapy remains unclear. We therefore investigated their associations with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) lesion reversal, hemorrhagic complications, and short-term functional outcome after MRI-guided reperfusion therapy. METHODS: In this retrospective single-center study, consecutive patients with acute ischemic stroke undergoing MRI-guided intravenous thrombolysis, with or without additional mechanical thrombectomy, were included. According to the institutional protocol, follow-up MRI was planned 24 ± 6 h after treatment to assess DWI lesion evolution, WMH volume, and CMBs. DWI reversal was defined as a reduction of ≥ 25% in baseline DWI lesion volume. Multivariable regression analyses were performed to identify predictors of DWI reversal, intracerebral hemorrhage, and functional outcome at hospital discharge. RESULTS: Among 345 patients (median age 74 years [IQR 63-82], 48.1% female), 45 (13%) additionally underwent mechanical thrombectomy. DWI reversal occurred in 76 patients (22.0%) and was not associated with baseline WMH volume, CMBs, initial infarct volume, treatment modality, or thrombolysis time window. Higher baseline NIHSS and modified Rankin Scale scores were associated with lower odds of DWI reversal, whereas hypercholesterolemia was independently associated with increased odds of DWI reversal. We found no evidence of an association of WMH burden or CMB presence with intracerebral hemorrhage or of an independent association with functional outcome. Fourteen patients (4.1%) developed new CMBs on follow-up MRI. CONCLUSIONS: We found no evidence of an association between baseline WMH volume or CMB presence and early DWI lesion reversal or hemorrhagic complications following reperfusion therapy in this cohort. These findings provide no evidence that these two chronic MRI markers are major determinants of early infarct tissue reversibility. Larger multicenter studies incorporating comprehensive small-vessel disease phenotyping and long-term follow-up are warranted.

title: Panax notoginseng -Derived Carbon Quantum Dots as a Novel Administration Strategy for Cerebral Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury Therapy.
abstract: Panax notoginseng Panax notoginseng Panax notoginseng The present study aimed to synthesize-derived carbon quantum dots (PN-CDs) and explore their role in cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI). PN-CDs were synthesized by the hydrothermal method, and characterization and biocompatibility were assessed. Next, CIRI models were established using SH-SY5Y cells, primary neurons were treated with oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R), and rats were subjected to middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO/R). After PN-CDs treatment, inflammation, apoptosis, and oxidative stress were detected in neuronal cells and rats using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction, flow cytometry, Western blot, and 2',7'-dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate probe. Meanwhile, 2,3,5-triphenyltetrazolium chloride, terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling, Nissl, and hematoxylin and eosin staining were employed to measure the pathological damage of rats. Additionally, CIRI rats were administered with PN-CDs,saponins (PNS),(PN), or edaravone to investigate whether PN-CDs had the best effect. The findings revealed that PN-CDs exhibited favorable biocompatibility and crossed the blood-brain barrier. In vitro, PN-CD treatment inhibited oxidative stress, apoptosis, and inflammation, as evidenced by the decrease of interleukin-1β (IL-1β), IL-6, Bax, C-caspase-3, tumor necrosis factor-α, malondialdehyde, and reactive oxygen species and the increase of superoxide dismutase, Bcl-2, and glutathione. In CIRI rats, PN-CDs improved pathological damage and suppressed inflammation, apoptosis, and oxidative stress. The therapeutic effect of PN-CDs on CIRI was distinctly better than that of PNS and PN, and comparable to that of the first-line drug edaravone. In short, PN-CDs, a novel and efficient administration strategy, alleviates CIRI by inhibiting apoptosis, oxidative stress, and inflammation.

title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics reveal mesenchymal stem cell-associated neuroimmune and neuronal signaling patterns after ischemic stroke.
abstract: Ischemic stroke induces coordinated yet spatially heterogeneous neuroimmune and neuronal responses that shape secondary injury and tissue remodeling. However, how intranasal mesenchymal stem cell administration is associated with these cell type-specific responses remains incompletely understood. Here, we integrated single-cell RNA sequencing of the ipsilateral cerebrum on days 1, 7, and 14 after middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion with spatial transcriptomic profiling on day 7. A total of 55,520 high-quality single-cell transcriptomes were obtained from control, middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion, and mesenchymal stem cell-treated samples. In this exploratory dataset, the middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion samples showed relatively greater representation of inflammatory and antigen-presenting microglial states and elevated expression of selected microglial state-associated genes, including Slfn4, Apoe, and Gpnmb. In the corresponding exploratory comparison, the mesenchymal stem cell-treated sample showed relatively greater representation of homeostatic-associated and Lgals3/Spp1-enriched microglial states and lower expression of several inflammatory-associated genes. Spatial mapping further revealed regionally restricted expression of microglial and neuronal markers within the injured tissue. Excitatory neurons displayed preliminary mesenchymal stem cell-associated transcriptional patterns involving mitochondrial transcripts, oxidative phosphorylation, synaptic signaling, calcium-related functions, and apoptosis/autophagy-associated pathways. CellChat analysis computationally predicted relatively high levels of tumor necrosis factor, C-X-C motif chemokine ligand, and complement signaling in the middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion sample, whereas the mesenchymal stem cell-treated sample had relatively high levels of predicted activity of neuregulin, pleiotrophin and selected semaphorin. Together, these integrated datasets provide a hypothesis-generating framework linking microglial state remodeling, neuronal metabolic and synaptic programs, and predicted neuroimmune communication patterns after ischemic stroke. Because each omics condition or time point was represented by one biological sample, all the transcriptomic findings should be considered preliminary and exploratory and should be validated in independently replicated cohorts.

title: Engineering a Translational Human Thrombus Platform to Evaluate Clinical Therapies in Ischemic Stroke.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Recanalization failure after ischemic stroke remains a major clinical challenge, partly because cerebral thrombi display marked spatial heterogeneity that is poorly reproduced by experimental models. Here, we engineered a translational human blood-based thrombus platform that recapitulates key histological features of patient-derived stroke clots. METHODS: Under controlled conditions, the platform generated reproducible thrombi with pronounced interthrombus and intrathrombus heterogeneity, including alternating red blood cell-rich and platelet-rich territories. Multiscale structural and biochemical analyses confirmed the successful replication of the clinical biphasic organization associated with resistance to rtPA (recombinant tissue-type plasminogen activator): a compact outer fibrin shell containing focal accumulations of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1, and a dense inner core further stabilized by neutrophil extracellular traps. RESULTS: Functional thrombolysis assays demonstrated that this architecture directly dictates lytic susceptibility. Specifically, artificially breaching the outer fibrin shell (halved thrombi) significantly accelerated early rtPA-mediated lysis, proving its role as an effective physical barrier. Furthermore, lytic response was inherently linked to clot composition: platelet-rich thrombi with dense plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 and neutrophil extracellular trap networks exhibited profound resistance to standard rtPA compared with red blood cell-rich clots. Supporting the platform's translational relevance, this structural resistance was successfully overcome by clinically relevant strategies, including tenecteplase and adjunctive DNAse, consistent with observations from human stroke cohorts. CONCLUSIONS: By accurately reproducing the spatial organization and differential thrombolytic responses of human cerebral thrombi, this translational framework provides a robust preclinical tool to dissect lytic resistance and evaluate next-generation precision reperfusion therapies. Furthermore, developing robust ex vivo human platforms is increasingly critical to align with the replacement, reduction, refinement ethical guidelines for animal research.

title: Advances in research and clinical decision strategies for anticoagulation timing in acute ischemic stroke patients with atrial fibrillation.
abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a major risk factor for acute ischemic stroke (AIS), and oral anticoagulation is the cornerstone of secondary prevention. The optimal timing of anticoagulation initiation remains controversial because of the need to balance the risks of early ischemic recurrence and hemorrhagic transformation. Recent randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses indicate that early initiation of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) is generally safe in appropriately selected patients and may reduce recurrent ischemic events without increasing the risk of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage. However, evidence remains limited in patients with severe stroke, hemorrhagic transformation, large infarcts, or recent reperfusion therapy, in whom the timing of anticoagulation should be individualized according to clinical and neuroimaging characteristics. The 2026 AHA/ASA guideline considers early oral anticoagulation reasonable in carefully selected patients with AIS and AF, particularly those with milder stroke severity, without specifying a uniform initiation window. Clinical decision-making should integrate stroke severity, neuroimaging findings, and individual thromboembolic and bleeding risks. Overall, current evidence supports a shift from fixed delay rules toward individualized anticoagulation strategies.

title: Intranasal Delivery of an Antioxidant Nanoassembly for Cerebral Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury via Drd2/β-arrestin2/ERK Signaling.
abstract: Cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) is caused by reduced cerebral blood flow, leading to excessive oxidative stress and neurological deficits. Curcumin (Cur) is a promising therapeutic agent, but its antioxidant activity is limited by low bioavailability and poor brain penetration. Herein, an intranasal delivery strategy using a tetrahedral framework nucleic acid (tFNAs)-Cur nanoassembly (tFNAs-Cur) was employed for CIRI treatment. tFNAs-Cur was synthesized through self-assembly, achieving a high Cur loading efficiency of 87% and exhibiting potent scavenging activity against reactive oxygen species (ROS) including O2·-, ·OH, and H2O2. In vitro studies showed that tFNAs-Cur inhibited oxygen glucose deprivation/reoxygenation-induced ROS elevation of cytoplasm and mitochondria, and enhanced proliferation and migration of SH-SY5Y cells. In vivo studies demonstrated that intranasal administration of tFNAs-Cur reduced cerebral infarct volume, enhanced neuronal survival, and improved neurological and behavioral outcomes in middle cerebral artery occlusion rats. Further mechanistic investigation using RNA sequencing revealed that tFNAs-Cur exerted its effects by activating the Drd2/β-arrestin2/ERK signaling, thereby improving mitochondrial function and upregulating BDNF levels. Furthermore, hemolysis assays, serum biochemical measurements, and histopathological analyses demonstrated that tFNAs-Cur possessed a favorable biosafety profile both ex vivo and in vivo. This study provides an intranasal antioxidant nanoassembly strategy for CIRI and holds potential for clinical translation.

title: RIC-specific cytoprotective profile mediated by microglia in a mouse model of acute ischaemic stroke.
abstract: Background: Remote ischaemic conditioning (RIC) is an endogenous neuroprotective strategy involving repeated, transient occlusion of a limb artery to reduce ischaemic injury at a distant site. We investigated the effects of RIC in a mouse model of focal cerebral ischaemia induced by distal transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO). Animals were randomised into three groups: Stroke (tMCAO, 60 min), Stroke+remote ischaemic preconditioning (RIPerC) (RIC applied during ischaemia) and Stroke+remote ischaemic postconditioning (RIPostC) (RIC initiated 10 min after reperfusion). The RIC protocol consisted of three cycles of 5-minute hindlimb ischaemia followed by 5-minute reperfusion. Results: At 72 hours postischaemia, both RIPerC and RIPostC significantly reduced the infarct volumes in male and female mice. In males, infarct size decreased from 6.31 ± 0.28% (Stroke) to 3.77 ± 0.47% (RIPerC, p<0.0025) and 4.00 ± 0.40% (RIPostC, p<0.0061). However, the RIPerC+RIPostC group significantly increased the infarct volume compared with the Stroke group (8.41± 0.72%). In females, reductions were greater: from 6.69±0.46% (Stroke) to 2.95 ± 0.34% (RIPerC, p<0.0001) and 2.96 ± 0.32% (RIPostC, p<0.0001). Functional recovery was improved, particularly with RIPostC, correlating with infarct size reduction (Pearson’s r=0.5505 in males, r=0.7313 in females). Apoptosis was reduced by over 50% with both treatments, and microglial phagocytic activity (cluster of differentiation 68+/Iba1+ (ionised calcium binding adaptor molecule 1)) increased significantly. Microglial depletion using PLX3397 (71.3% reduction in Iba1+ cells) worsened ischaemic injury, yet RIC preserved its protective effects, suggesting additional microglia-independent mechanisms. Furthermore, RIC enhanced neurogenesis in the subventricular zone and infarct core (doublecortin marker+ cells doubled versus Stroke), with a marked proliferative response in female hippocampi (Ki67+ cells increased by 127%). Conclusion: These findings reveal sex-specific efficacy of RIC, with mechanistic insights obtained in male animals suggesting a dual mode of action via modulation of microglial function and promotion of endogenous neurorepair pathways.

title: Sequential blood-brain barrier-penetrating and microglial-mitochondria-targeting nanosystem for ischemic stroke therapy.
abstract: Ischemic stroke (IS) causes severe neurological deficits closely linked to microglial overactivation after ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury, a process governed by mitochondrial homeostasis. However, restoring microglial mitochondrial function across the blood-brain barrier (BBB) remains challenging. Here, we report a sequentially targeted nanosystem, M-BPM@TGPB, for I/R injury therapy. It comprises a triphenylphosphonium (TPP)-modified, gadolinium-doped Prussian blue core and a mannose-modified BV2-platelet hybrid membrane shell. This design integrates mannose for BBB penetration, platelet membrane for lesion targeting, BV2 membrane for microglial uptake, and TPP for mitochondrial localization, enabling precise vascular-to-subcellular delivery. In vitro, the nanosystem crossed the BBB, localized to BV2 mitochondria, scavenged reactive oxygen species (ROS), restored mitochondrial function, and inhibited inflammation. In a mouse model of middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO/R), the intravenously administered nanosystem accumulated in microglial mitochondria, scavenged mitochondrial ROS (mtROS), restored mitochondrial homeostasis, promoted M1-to-M2 polarization, suppressed neuroinflammation, reduced neuronal apoptosis, and promoted angiogenesis, thereby reducing infarct volume from 36.61% to 10.57% and the modified neurological severity score (mNSS) from 14 to 2.5. It also exhibited favorable biocompatibility and enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) contrast. Critically, rather than broadly scavenging ROS, this strategy specifically restores microglial mitochondrial function, shifting the therapeutic focus from general antioxidant approaches to organelle-specific intervention. This work may offer a promising design paradigm for nanotherapies targeting central nervous system disorders in which mitochondrial dysfunction and neuroinflammation are core pathological drivers.

title: Beyond Blood-Brain Barrier Crossing in Reperfusion-Era Ischemic Stroke: Interface-Matched Active-Entity Delivery and Translational Product Design.
abstract: Reperfusion therapy has transformed acute ischemic stroke care, yet large-vessel recanalization does not ensure capillary reperfusion, preservation of the blood-brain barrier and neurovascular unit (BBB/NVU), or durable neurological recovery. Nanomedicine is still commonly judged by BBB crossing or ischemic-hemisphere accumulation, although vascular access, tissue viability, transport phenotype, thromboinflammation, and standard treatment change rapidly during the lifetime of a formulation. This narrative review proposes a conceptual framework that matches the reperfusion state and pathological interface to the compartment in which the therapeutically active entity must act. The framework is intended to organize preclinical evidence and generate testable translational hypotheses; it has not yet been clinically validated. Persistent occlusion may favor intravascular targets, whereas recanalization with no-reflow creates a distinct microvascular delivery problem. Early reperfusion injury may prioritize BBB/NVU stabilization, while later biological contexts may require selective immune, regenerative, or organelle-directed interventions. These contexts may coexist spatially, vary across vascular territories, and shift during treatment; they should therefore not be interpreted as a mandatory chronological sequence. We distinguish BBB crossing, controlled barrier modulation, and BBB/NVU repair as separate therapeutic tasks, and introduce transport attrition as a practical explanation for why sequential targeting, transcytosis, cellular uptake, endosomal escape, and organelle localization can yield little final active-entity exposure despite strong tissue imaging. Recent predominantly preclinical examples illustrate how thrombus-targeted rtPA systems, neutrophil-intercepting particles, NET-degrading polymersomes, lesion-targeted nanoplatforms, and mitochondrial nanomedicines may fit different delivery topologies. Translational credibility requires topology-resolved exposure, target engagement in viable tissue, hemocompatibility under antithrombotic treatment, state-appropriate models, function-linked manufacturing controls, and compatibility with thrombolysis and thrombectomy.

title: Mitochondrial cristae remodeling in ischemic stroke: mechanisms and therapeutic perspectives.
abstract: Mitochondrial cristae arrange the respiratory machinery within the inner membrane and change as ischemia gives way to reperfusion. Their organization depends on mitochondrial contact site and cristae organizing system assemblies, optic atrophy 1, adenosine triphosphate synthase, and cardiolipin. Disruption of these systems can impair energy production, facilitate neuronal death, and expose mitochondrial DNA to inflammatory sensors. This review brings structural work together with experimental stroke studies to examine how crista remodeling contributes to injury and recovery. Genetic manipulation of selected regulators has preserved mitochondrial structure and reduced injury in neurons and microglia. Most of these interventions preceded ischemia, leaving the speed and feasibility of repair after stroke onset uncertain. Pharmacological modulation and mitochondrial delivery offer ways to address this gap, particularly around reperfusion. Emerging strategies combine modulation of crista protein assemblies with cardiolipin directed treatment, mitochondrial antioxidant nanomedicine, organelle delivery, and control of local drug exposure. Their therapeutic evaluation can be aligned with distinct opportunities at reperfusion and during subsequent tissue recovery. Progress toward treatment will require evidence that a candidate reaches the affected brain cells, modifies the intended membrane assembly, and produces lasting neurological benefit. The available studies place crista remodeling within neuroprotective pathways and identify the experimental steps needed to evaluate it as a therapeutic target.

title: Characterization and treatment of ischemic stroke in patients with infective endocarditis: a meta-analysis.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Ischemic stroke is a common and serious complication of infective bacterial endocarditis. This study aimed to characterize the frequency, clinical and pathological features, treatment strategies, and outcomes of patients with stroke due to infective endocarditis. METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed from database inception to October 2022 for studies reporting on stroke in patients with infective endocarditis and performed a meta-analysis. RESULTS: A total of 122 studies comprising 270,211 patients with infective endocarditis were included. Ischemic stroke occurred in 21% and hemorrhagic stroke in 5% of patients. Stroke was observed in 32% of patients with mitral valve endocarditis, 25% with aortic valve, and 11% with tricuspid valve endocarditis. Stroke was associated with significantly higher mortality (OR 2.35; 95%CI 1.74-3.16). Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species were most frequently associated with stroke (33% and 25%, respectively). The risk of stroke did not differ significantly between patients with and without pre-existing antithrombotic therapy (37% vs. 24%; OR 1.24, 95%CI 0.75-2.06). Successful reperfusion was achieved in 80% of patients undergoing mechanical thrombectomy, although mortality remained high at 49%. CONCLUSIONS: Stroke is a common complication of infective bacterial endocarditis and has a substantial impact on patient outcomes. It occurs most frequently in patients with mitral valve endocarditis and in those with infections caused by staphylococcal pathogens. Stroke risk was not reduced in patients with pre-existing antithrombotic therapy, supporting discontinuation where no other indication exists. Mechanical thrombectomy in patients with endocarditis-related large vessel occlusion achieves high recanalization rates; however, overall clinical outcomes remain poor in this population.

title: Neutrophil extracellular traps in ischemic stroke: Thrombolysis resistance, no-reflow, and hemorrhagic transformation.
abstract: Recanalization is central to acute ischemic stroke treatment. However, reopening an occluded artery does not always restore microvascular perfusion, and hemorrhagic transformation (HT) can occur regardless of recanalization success. Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) may help explain these discordant outcomes because they act within occlusive thrombi, the downstream microcirculation, and the neurovascular interface. This review examines the roles of NETs in thrombolysis resistance, no-reflow, and hemorrhagic injury. Within thrombi, NET-associated chromatin reinforces clot architecture and limits fibrinolysis. Intravascular NETs may impede downstream microvascular flow after recanalization, while NET-related inflammatory signaling may aggravate blood-brain barrier disruption and HT. These findings implicate NETs in impaired recanalization, incomplete tissue reperfusion, and hemorrhagic injury and support their evaluation as an adjunctive target during reperfusion therapy.

title: Mitochondrial calpain-1 cleaves MAVS and controls inflammation in cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury.
abstract: Calpains are calcium-activated cysteine proteases present in the cytoplasm and mitochondria that are essential to physiological processes; however, the functions of calpain-1 in the brain are not well understood. Therefore, we explored novel calpain-1 substrates using the GPS-CCD software package. Calpain inhibitors, calpeptin and Tat-μCL, suppressed cleavage of mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS) in the presence of exogenous calcium. Moreover, calpain-1 knockout mice suppressed MAVS cleavage in cerebral ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury. These findings indicate that MAVS is a novel calpain-1 substrate. As MAVS degradation prevents inflammation, its cleavage might contribute to the suppression of inflammation in I/R injury.

title: Calycosin alleviates blood-brain barrier disruption after cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury by inhibiting NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis.
abstract: Ischemic stroke, a severe neurological disorder with a multifactorial pathogenesis, presents significant therapeutic challenges. Calycosin, a natural flavonoid, has diverse biological activities, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antitumor effects. In this study we investigate the protective effects of calycosin against blood-brain barrier (BBB) damage following cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) and explore the underlying mechanisms. We employ middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) in rats and oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD) in bEnd.3 brain microvascular endothelial cells to assess neurological function, BBB integrity, the expression of pyroptosis-related proteins, inflammatory mediator release, endothelial barrier permeability, and cell viability. The results reveal that calycosin significantly ameliorates CIRI-induced BBB damage, as evidenced by improved neurological scores, reduced brain water content, and decreased infarct volume. Calycosin suppresses NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis by downregulating HMGB1, NLRP3, caspase 1, GSDMD, N-GSDMD, and IL-18 expression while reducing the secretion of HMGB1, IL-1β, and IL-18. Additionally, calycosin enhances BBB integrity by decreasing MMP9 and AQP-4 expression and upregulating the expression of tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin, and claudin-5). In OGD-treated bEnd.3 cells, calycosin inhibits NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis, reduces inflammatory mediator release, and improves cell viability and barrier function. Notably, molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations demonstrate that calycosin stably binds to NLRP3 with high affinity, supporting its potential as an NLRP3 inhibitor. These findings indicate that calycosin protects against CIRI-induced BBB damage by inhibiting NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis and modulating tight junction protein expression, indicating that calycosin is a potential therapeutic option for ischemic stroke.

title: [Acute management of minor ischemic stroke].
abstract: This review summarizes acute-phase treatment for minor ischemic stroke, focusing on the latest evidence for reperfusion therapy and acute antithrombotic treatment. In patients with large vessel occlusion, the benefit of mechanical thrombectomy is not established and the risk of hemorrhage exists; therefore, indications should be judged carefully for each patient. Intravenous thrombolysis provides limited benefit in non-disabling cases, and dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) can be an option. For minor non-cardioembolic stroke, early DAPT is recommended, and the possible role of adding argatroban is promising, especially for suspected branch atheromatous disease. For cardioembolic stroke, early initiation of a direct oral anticoagulant is desirable in mild cases without a large infarct.

title: Neuroprotective effect by splenic hypothermia in ischemic stroke.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To investigate whether spleen-targeted remote administration of hypothermia (RAH) modulates splenic neutrophil release, attenuates neutrophil-driven cerebral inflammation, and preserves BBB integrity at early reperfusion after stroke. METHODS: Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent 2-h middle cerebral artery occlusion followed by 6-, 24- and 48- h of reperfusion. RAH was applied to the splenic region via surface cooling, with 1-min cycles administered at 5-min intervals. Neurological deficits, infarct volume, neutrophil infiltration, cytokine expression, BBB integrity, and apoptosis were assessed using neurobehavioral scoring, TTC staining, Western blotting, rt-PCR, immunofluorescence, ELISA, and TUNEL, respectively. RESULTS: 0 RAH rapidly reduced splenic temperature from 37to 28 °C without altering body or brain temperatures. At 6 h reperfusion, splenic neutrophil release was suppressed and brain neutrophil infiltration decreased. RAH reduced early elevations of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6. At 24 h, anti-inflammatory effects persisted and BBB integrity was preserved, restoring tight-junction and matrix proteins and suppressing BBB-damaging mediators. Compared to non-RAH stroked rats, RAH reduced apoptosis, body weight loss (9.1 ± 2.8 vs. 19.7 ± 7.2 g, p < 0.05), infarct volume (33.9 ± 4.1% vs. 53.6 ± 1.9%, p < 0.05), cerebral edema (11.2 ± 0.9% vs. 16.3 ± 1.3%, p < 0.05) and Evans blue extravasation (4.8 ± 0.2 vs. 9.8 ± 0.2 mg/g, p < 0.05), and improved neurological outcomes. RAH attenuated stroke-induced spleen weight loss and contraction, consistent with reduced splenic neutrophil mobilization. CONCLUSIONS: RAH induces neuroprotection after ischemic stroke by suppressing splenic neutrophil activation and mobilization, thus attenuating peripheral-to-central inflammatory trafficking and preserving BBB integrity. These findings highlight spleen-targeted cooling may represent a promising early intervention to ischemic stroke.

title: Mechanisms of Spns2 in regulating neuroinflammatory activation of microglia after cerebral ischemia in rats.
abstract: Microglia, the resident innate immune cells of the brain, maintain central nervous system homeostasis but can also mediate inflammatory injury after ischemic stroke. Following ischemia, microglia can adopt pro-inflammatory M1- or reparative M2-like state; thus, regulating the balance between these phenotypes may be therapeutically relevant. Sphingosine-1-phosphate signaling regulates immune responses, angiogenesis, and endothelial barrier integrity. Enhanced sphingosine-1-phosphate signaling in activated microglia after ischemic injury may amplify inflammatory cascades. However, strategies targeting sphingosine-1-phosphate signaling are constrained by the heterogeneous expression of sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors. Spinster homolog 2 (Spns2), a sphingosine-1-phosphate exporter, may provide an alternative target, although its role in ischemic stroke remains unclear. To investigate the role of Spns2 in post-ischemic neuroinflammation, middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion was induced in Spns2-deficient (Spns2-/-) and wild-type rats. BV2 microglial cells exposed to oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation were used as an in vitro model. Spns2 mRNA expression in the peri-infarct penumbra increased after middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion and peaked at 24 hours. Compared with wild-type rats, Spns2-/- rats showed lower neurological deficit scores, improved motor performance, and smaller infarct volumes. In the peri-infarct penumbra, Spns2 deficiency was associated with decreased expression of pro-inflammatory markers, increased expression of anti-inflammatory markers, and attenuated microglia-associated NOD-like receptor pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome signaling. In BV2 cells, Spns2 knockdown produced similar changes in inflammatory-marker expression and reduced oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation-induced NLRP3 inflammasome-associated signaling and oxidative stress. Spns2 knockdown reduced extracellular sphingosine-1-phosphate levels in BV2-cell culture supernatants, whereas exogenous sphingosine-1-phosphate supplementation increased the expression of inflammasome-associated inflammatory mediators in Spns2-knockdown BV2 cells. RNA sequencing identified Itga5 upregulation in Spns2-/- rats and showed that differentially expressed genes between Spns2-/- and wild-type rats were enriched in the phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B (Akt) signaling pathway. Increased Akt phosphorylation in Spns2-/- rats was further confirmed by western blotting. These findings indicate that Spns2 deficiency limits sphingosine-1-phosphate export and attenuates microglia-associated neuroinflammation after ischemic stroke. Itga5 upregulation and increased Akt phosphorylation may be associated with this neuroprotective effect. Collectively, our results provide a basis for further investigation of the Spns2-sphingosine-1-phosphate axis in ischemic stroke.

title: Oleanolic acid-hesperetin co-assembled nanoparticles alleviate neurological injury after ischemic stroke via the PI3K/AKT/GSK-3β axis.
abstract: Ischemic stroke remains a leading cause of death and long-term disability, while the current clinically applicable adjunctive neuroprotective strategies face substantial limitations. Oleanolic acid and hesperetin exhibit synergistic antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-apoptotic activities; however, their poor aqueous solubility and limited bioavailability remain major limitations to their therapeutic development. Oleanolic acid and hesperetin were formulated as co-assembled nanoparticles using an emulsion-solvent evaporation method. A 5:2 mass ratio of oleanolic acid to hesperetin produced primarily spherical nanoparticles with a mean hydrodynamic diameter of approximately 282.6 nm, a polydispersity index of 0.197, and a zeta potential of -12.2 mV. Oleanolic acid-hesperetin nanoparticles displayed minimal hemolysis (0.199%) while maintaining a stable hydrodynamic diameter during 30 days of storage. Spectroscopic analyses and a 50 ns molecular dynamics simulation promoted co-assembly via multiple noncovalent-driven interactions. Oleanolic acid-hesperetin nanoparticles effectively reduced oxygen-glucose deprivation/reperfusion-induced viability loss and apoptosis in HT22 cells. In transient middle cerebral artery occlusion mice, Cy5.5-associated fluorescence was observed in brain tissue, whereas oleanolic acid-hesperetin nanoparticle treatment reduced infarct volume and ipsilesional brain water content, preserved neurons, resulting in improved sensorimotor and spatial cognitive outcomes through day 28. Treatment promoted PI3K and AKT phosphorylation, elevated inhibitory phosphorylation of glycogen synthase kinase 3β at Ser9 and BCL-2 expression, and reduced BAX expression. These findings suggest that oleanolic acid-hesperetin co-assembly offers a promising preclinical formulation approach for multifactorial neuroprotection after ischemic stroke and supports further pharmacokinetic, safety, and pathway-causality studies.

title: Development of a biomimetic manganese dioxide nanoreactor delivery system: Combination of biomimetic platelet/M2 microglia hybrid membrane with Astragaloside IV for the treatment of ischemic stroke.
abstract: Conventional nanotherapeutics suffer from rapid immune clearance and insufficient accumulation in ischemic lesions. To overcome these bottlenecks, a stimuli-responsive biomimetic immunomodulatory delivery system was engineered by fusing platelet and M2 microglial membranes onto hollow mesoporous manganese dioxide nanoparticles loaded with the neuroprotective drug Astragaloside IV. The results show that this integrated nanoplatform fully leverages the synergistic properties of its biomimetic shell. Tracing the nanoparticles with the fluorescent dye Did revealed that the integrated nanoplatform exhibited more pronounced fluorescent enrichment in ischemic brain tissue; both in vivo and ex vivo imaging supported its specific homing ability. In a mouse model of middle cerebral artery occlusion and reperfusion, the platform significantly reduced the extent of cerebral infarction, alleviated neuronal damage caused by ischemia-reperfusion, and improved neurovascular integrity and neurological function. Furthermore, the platform mitigated oxidative stress in ischemic brain tissue, curtailed the inflammatory response, and facilitated a transition in microglial phenotype toward an anti-inflammatory and reparative state. Bioinformatics results indicate that this platform significantly alters gene expression profiles following cerebral ischemia-reperfusion. Differential expression and functional enrichment analyses further point to biological processes related to inflammation and immune regulation. These findings demonstrate that this biomimetic targeted nanoplatform integrates biomimetic targeting, reactive oxygen species scavenging, and immune modulation capabilities, thereby providing a new therapeutic platform technology for the precise delivery of therapeutic agents and the remodeling of the pathological microenvironment in ischemic stroke.

To overcome these bottlenecks, a stimuli-responsive biomimetic immunomodulatory delivery system was engineered by fusing platelet and M2 microglial membranes onto hollow mesoporous manganese dioxide nanoparticles loaded with the neuroprotective drug Astragaloside IV. The results show that this integrated nanoplatform fully leverages the synergistic properties of its biomimetic shell.
